candidates.name: Yūshūkan War Memorial Museum
candidates.price: Adult ¥1000, post-secondary student ¥500, high school student ¥300, child free

candidates.price: Park admission ¥300 (age 65+ ¥150, primary school children free)

candidates.name: Toyosu Market
candidates.hours: Mon-Sat 05:00-17:00; closed holidays and most Wednesdays
candidates.content: Toyosu is new home of the world's largest wholesale market for seafood and produce after its relocation from Tsukiji. Unlike the old facility where tourists could almost walk up to the fish, Toyosu's market has large enclosed obse

candidates.name: Fukagawa Edo Museum
candidates.alt: 深川江戸資料館, fukagawa edo shiryōkan
candidates.content: This intimate museum features a wonderfully recreated Tempo-period (1830-1843) neighbourhood - complete with homes, shops, narrow alleyways, and even the local rubbish dump. Wander about, peering in windows and entering buildings

candidates.name: Ship Lucky Dragon 5
candidates.content: The restored fishing boat Lucky Dragon the crew of which became unfortunate victims of nuclear fallout fallowing a thermonuclear test at Bikini Atoll is on display at Tokyo Metropolitan Daigo Fukuryū Maru Exhibition Hall. On 1 Mar

candidates.name: TEPIA
candidates.content: Science museum showcasing new technologies, robots, home automation. Explanations are in Japanese but playing with the objects is still fun for kids and adults.

candidates.name: National Art Center
candidates.price: Entry fees vary by exhibition, some are free
candidates.content: Tokyo's latest and greatest art museum, housed in an undulating wave-shaped building designed by Kisho Kurokawa and devoted entirely to changing exhibitions.

candidates.name: Mori Art Museum
candidates.content: This impressive art gallery hosts special exhibitions. The museum ticket includes admission to Tokyo City View. The Mori Arts Center Gallery adjacent to the Mori Art Museum requires separate admission (prices vary), not included w

candidates.name: Machiko Hasegawa Museum
candidates.alt: 長谷川町子美術館 Hasegawa machiko bijutsukan
candidates.price: Adults ¥600, college and high school students ¥500, junior high and elementary school students ¥400
candidates.content: Art museum dedicated to the works of Machiko Hasegawa, creator of Sazae-san, one of Japan's longest running comic strips and cartoons. Showcases include original drawings, clay dolls, and paintings.

candidates.name: Yamatane Museum of Art
candidates.content: Specializes in modern Japanese-style paintings and has a notable collection, though only a handful are on display at one time due to preservation issues.

candidates.name: Hara Museum of Contemporary Art
candidates.content: This small museum hosts a variety of interesting exhibitions in a 1930s house which is a great example of modern architecture in pre-war Japan. There is a very nice indoor/outdoor cafe. (2026: closed/moved to Gunma prefecture, see

candidates.name: Fire Museum
candidates.content: Three fire-fighting helicopters, ten trucks, and 3 floors of exhibitions. Very popular with kids, who can wear fire-fighting clothes and ride some of the helicopters and trucks.

candidates.name: Edo-Tokyo Museum
candidates.price: Adult ¥1,300, age 65 and over ¥650, university student with ID ¥1,040, younger students with ID free; ¥100 discount for advance purchase
candidates.hours: Tue-Sun 09:30 - 17:30, Sat 09:30 - 19:30; last admission 30 minutes before closing time
candidates.content: This bizarre multi-story edifice suspended in midair and bearing not a small resemblance to a Star Wars Imperial Walker (meant to be a replica of an old raised warehouse) covers the history of the metropolis, starting from 1590 wh

candidates.name: Japanese Sword Museum
candidates.content: Display of all types of Japanese art swords and fittings, some of them centuries old. Beautiful view from balcony on 3rd floor over Kyū Yasuda Garden. Quite hefty entrance fee, but a must see for anyone interested in Japanese swor

candidates.name: Sumo Museum
candidates.content: A small, quirky museum tucked inside the arena's first floor, dedicated to the history of sumo, particularly artifacts and ceremonial clothing, almost entirely in Japanese only. The collection rotates several times a year. During

candidates.name: Tobacco and Salt Museum
candidates.alt: たばこと塩の博物館 Tabako to Shio no Hakubutsukan
candidates.content: This peculiar institution owes its existence to Japan's government monopoly on these two substances. The website advises that "dangerous substances are not permitted within the museum". They have map-guides of the museum in Englis

candidates.name: Tobu Museum
candidates.content: A museum of railways and buses, operated by Tobu Railway. At the museum, visitors can also see trains running through Higashi Mukojima Station, which is located directly above the museum.

candidates.name: Asakura Museum of Sculpture
candidates.content: 20px|Must visit! Sculptor Asakura Fumio (Artist name Kōso 1883-1964) designed this atmospheric house himself. It combined his original Japanese home and garden with a large studio that incorporated vaulted ceilings, a 'sunrise roo

candidates.name: Shitamachi Museum Annex
candidates.alt: 下町風俗資料館付設展示場, shitamachifū-shiryōkan-fusetsu-tenjijō
candidates.hours: Tue-Sun 09:30-16:30, closed Mon, also Tue following a holiday. Closed until March 2025 for renovations
candidates.content: Many buildings scattered around the Yanaka district survived the bombings of World War II, including this former sake store built in 1910. Characteristic of Meiji-era architecture, the building now houses a small museum of sake an

candidates.name: National Museum of Western Art
candidates.alt: 国立西洋美術館, Kokuritsu Seiyō Bijutsukan
candidates.price: Entry ¥420; free admission on the 2nd and 4th Saturdays of each month
candidates.content: Houses an extensive collection of Western art, including the original of Rodin's famous The Thinker. It is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage as part of "The Architectural Work of Le Corbusier, an Outstanding Contribution to the Mo

candidates.name: Tokyo Midtown
candidates.content: Opened in April 2007, this competitor to Roppongi Hills boasts Tokyo's second tallest office building, a Ritz-Carlton and yet more endless acres of shopping and eating. Still, Midtown favors wood paneling and greenery over raw con

candidates.name: Suntory Museum of Art
candidates.content: Hosts changing art exhibitions.

candidates.name: St. Mary's Cathedral
candidates.alt: 東京カテドラル聖マリア大聖堂 Tokyo Cathedral
candidates.content: Seat of the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Tokyo. Designed by the famous architect Tange Kenzō, this ultramodern church was built in the 1960s to replace an older structure that was destroyed during the war.

candidates.name: Hijiri-bashi Bridge
candidates.content: On the Kanda river (神田川), on the border between Bunkyō and Chiyoda wards. It offers one of the best spots in Tokyo to see trains, three lines crossing each other (on the west, so better seen in the afternoon). Akihabara district i

candidates.name: Imperial Palace
candidates.content: Surrounded by a series of moats and high walls, the site of the former Edo Castle has been the official residence of the Japanese imperial family since 1868. Reputedly the most expensive square kilometre in the world, which during

candidates.name: Kitanomaru Park
candidates.content: Connected to the East Gardens on the north side is this park. Offering much of the same, it is a convenient way to get to Yasukuni Shrine. The park also houses the Nippon Budōkan (日本武道館), which regularly stages martial arts compet

candidates.name: Kabukiza Theater
candidates.content: The best way to see traditional Japanese theater is to go to Kabuki-za for a single act, or hitomaku-mi, which lasts between one and two hours. This costs around ¥800, depending on the length, and seating is on the fourth floo

candidates.name: Ryōgoku Kokugikan
candidates.price: Advance-booking Western-style chairs on the second floor are ¥3,600, ¥4,900 and ¥8,400; Japanese-style box seats on the first floor are ¥9,200, ¥10,300 and ¥11,300. These can be purchased at ticket outlets and convenience stores, starting the month before the match. The Japan Sumo Association has an official English website handling online ticket sales. You can also buy sumo tickets by reserving through specialized third-party online ticket sellers, which charge higher markups; while there are generally no issues, the Sumo Association discourages purchases from these sites. In the past, unsold seats have been sold on the day of the tournament, but in the mid-2020s this has not been the case as all seats usually sell out soon after tickets go on sale
candidates.content: The largest sumo arena in Japan with a capacity for 10,000 spectators, this is where grand tournaments or basho are held in January, May and September, starting on the second Sunday of the month. These tournaments last for 15 days

candidates.name: Hanayashiki
candidates.content: The oldest amusement park in Japan. Next to the Sensō-ji temple grounds is this small and somewhat lackluster carnival complex with rides, booths, and games. The neighborhood theatre specializes in showing classic Japanese films,

candidates.name: Tokyo Dome City
candidates.content: An attractions complex featuring a large indoor stadium, an amusement park, bowling alley, off-track betting center, and the LaQua shopping mall/spa (see Buy). Tokyo Dome is one of several Tokyo stadiums. It is home to the Yomiuri

candidates.name: Hikarigaoka Park
candidates.content: One of the larger parks in Tokyo. It was left over land from a U.S. military base. The park has extensive open, grassy areas for picnics, frisbee and the like. There is also a large public pool, and a gym, a bird-watching center,

candidates.name: Meiji Jingu Stadium
candidates.content: Known as Jingu Stadium. Can see university and professional baseball games. It is also famous for being a stadium for the Tokyo qualifying round of the National High School Baseball Tournament.

candidates.name: Namja Town
candidates.alt: ナンジャタウンホーム
candidates.content: The Namja Town has many attractions. For example there are some Japanese style haunted houses, interactive 1964 shooting games, egg-raising game (the whole process is quite similar to raising a child, where you will need to take t

candidates.name: Pirates of Tokyo Bay
candidates.alt: パイレーツ・オブ・東京湾
candidates.hours: Last Sun of each month, doors 19:00
candidates.content: Tokyo's long-running English and Japanese improv comedy group has performed unscripted shows at What the Dickens! since 2010. The international cast takes audience suggestions in both languages and builds scenes on the spot using

candidates.name: TV Asahi
candidates.content: Headquarters of the television network that created Doraemon. Visit the mini-museum, complete with full-size models of the Doraemon world and of other popular Japanese TV shows.

candidates.name: Japan National Stadium
candidates.content: Completed in 2019 as the main stadium for the Summer Games Tokyo 2020.

candidates.name: Baseball Hall of Fame and Museum
candidates.price: Adults ¥500, seniors ¥300, children ¥200; discounts for groups of 20 or more
candidates.hours: Mar-Sep: Tue-Sun 10:00-18:00, Oct-Feb: Tue-Sun 10:00-17:00, closed Dec 29-Jan 1

candidates.name: Spa LaQua
candidates.price: ¥3,230/2,640 adult/child on weekdays, weekends +¥990, nights +¥2420 after 1am

candidates.name: Ramen Cooking Tokyo
candidates.content: English-only small-group cooking class (maximum 8 participants) where visitors prepare ramen and sushi in a 3-hour session, with a sake pairing of three varieties. Located in Tsukishima, a short walk from the monja-yaki district.

candidates.name: Tokyo Regional Immigration Bureau
candidates.alt: 東京出入国在留管理局
candidates.content: This center serves foreign residents and long-term visitors. Also houses immigration detention. If going in the morning, get there early because a line forms outside long before opening hours.

candidates.name: Niwa-no-yu
candidates.content: A large, upscale sento adjacent to Toshimaen which features indoor and outdoor baths, Roman steam rooms, Finnish saunas, a large indoor pool (bring your bathing suit), and an upstairs area with food, drinks, massages, and relaxati

candidates.name: Roppongi Hills Bon Odori & Azabujuban Noryo Festival
candidates.hours: Every year at the end of August 17:00-21:00 on Fri, Sat, Sun
candidates.content: Locals dance around drums in Japanese yukata dress in the Arena part of Roppongi Hills, expect Doraemon to make a surprise appearance to the delight of the kids. Continue your walk to the adjacent Azabujuban main street where all

candidates.name: Tollywood
candidates.content: This small theater (46 seats) specializes in independent short films, mostly Japanese. The films aren't dubbed or subtitled of course, but they're so offbeat and often bizarre that you're sure to have a good time anyway.

candidates.name: Ōi Horse Race Course
candidates.alt: 大井競馬場, Tokyo City Keiba
candidates.content: The best racecourse affiliated to National Association of Racing, the umbrella organization for local horseracing operators. Tokyo Dai-Shoten race in December is rated as international Grade I. Many restaurants and food stands. Ni

candidates.name: Yurikamome elevated train
candidates.price: max ¥390 each way; \820 one day pass
candidates.content: Take the Yurikamome elevated train across the bay bridge from Shimbashi station to the bayside Odaiba district, and take in the scenic view of the metropolis, including a giant Unicorn Gundam robot statue. A great experience durin

candidates.name: Shinjuku Piccadilly
candidates.content: The newest movie theater in Shinjuku. It features stadium seating and "platinum" seating. Platinum seating ranges from a semi-private room, including a private lounge (¥5000 per person) to a private room, including a relaxation ro

candidates.name: @home cafe
candidates.content: This maid cafe has card games, drinks, food, and young women dressed up as maids to serve you. If you order an omelet, they'll draw a picture of a cute animal on the top in ketchup. In addition to this shop, there are 3 branch sto

candidates.name: Kamiya Bar
candidates.content: The home of the Denki Bran cocktail, this was Japan's first Western-style bar when it first opened in 1880 and remains a truly local institution. The ground floor is a large beer-hall-like bar, the second is a Western-style restau

candidates.name: Cartagena
candidates.price: Beer, rum and others start at ¥500
candidates.content: A cozy and friendly spot where you can dance and drink. It is probably the first Latin bar in Nerima. The owner is a lady who once lived in Colombia; she speaks English and Spanish. There is a salsa event on weekends.

candidates.name: Abbott's Choice
candidates.content: Small, decent bar with NYC pop radio. Attracts a nice mix of tourists, expats and locals. A really welcome respite from the overpriced and overrated bars in the surrounding area.

candidates.name: Bar Quest Roppongi
candidates.content: Serves a selection of Aussie lagers including VB, Crown Lager and Coopers, cocktails and meat pies. A big-screen TV and a wide range of music played by DJs provide ongoing entertain­ment. You can also kick back Australian-style al

candidates.name: Shot Bar Propaganda
candidates.price: Drinks ¥800–1000 (half price before 21:00), no cover charge
candidates.content: An appropriately grubby joint decorated with propaganda posters and booming bass, playing mostly recent hits. While best known for its shots (check out the leaderboards!), their other drinks are pretty decent too and they have qui

candidates.name: Beat Cafe
candidates.price: Cash only and drinks range from ¥500-1000
candidates.content: Small cafe-bar-restaurant catering to the young alternative rock crowd. While showing constant videos from VH1 Classic on their TV, the easy drinking, simple eating crowd is about as friendly as they come. If you can't talk in you

candidates.name: Rock West
candidates.price: Cover charge of ¥1000 and most drinks around ¥500
candidates.content: A smaller, friendly club that specialised in underground techno, fairly well hidden on 7F of an office building. It's certainly one of the cheaper spots in the area.

candidates.name: Hair of The Dogs
candidates.content: Punk rock with a dash of Mexican Luchadors. Good cocktails and beer at an average of ¥700 a drink. The owner, Tohru, is very welcoming to anyone who loves to rock. Cover charge lets you sit at the bar and choose music from a menu

candidates.name: Bar Albatross-G
candidates.content: Casual cocktail bar with Burgundy painted walls, chandeliers and no-frills mixology. Cover charge includes a small snack of either noodles, miso or whatever's brewing. Most drinks are around ¥700. Space includes a second floor "at

candidates.name: New York Bar & Grill
candidates.content: One of the main sets for Lost in Translation, this slick joint on the 52nd floor has dark decor and floor-to-ceiling windows with jaw-dropping vistas, with live jazz nightly. Eating a steak here would cost you well north of ¥2

candidates.name: Loft/Plus One
candidates.content: Performance art space meets bar run with a simple concept: different people and groups rent a block of time and do whatever they want to. The end result runs from stand-up comedy and lectures to porn star photo shoots and incredib

candidates.name: Gold Finger
candidates.content: Primarily lesbian bar with all-female staff, and karaoke for the multinational patrons. Interior themed like a 1970s motel. Saturday is strictly women-only; Monday is FtM night.

candidates.name: Popeye Beer Club
candidates.price: Pints of beer are around ¥900, half pints and a sampler set are available
candidates.content: Popeye's is an excellent place to try Japanese microbrews. There are 70 beers on tap, which cover the full range of beers from familiar ales to barley wines and rauchbiers. The food menu is interesting, try the avocado and blue ch

candidates.name: Kagetsudo
candidates.content: This place has been making "melon pan" since 1945, and they haven't changed the decoration. It is a buttery and milky small cake with a crispy sweet crust.

candidates.name: Komagata Dozeu
candidates.content: Another local institution, Komagata has been serving up loach hotpot (dojō nabe) for over 200 years. Small, bony and slimy, loach was the working man's alternative to eel, then as now an expensive luxury. It's a bit of an acquired

candidates.name: Kanda Yabu soba
candidates.content: Yabu Soba opened its doors for business in 1880.

candidates.name: RyuGin
candidates.content: Moved from Roppongi in 2018. Combining a deep respect for the Japanese culinary heritage with a will to pushing boundaries has made Nihonryori RyuGin to regarded as one of the world's best restaurants. Serves a daily-changing fix

candidates.name: Oshio Honten
candidates.content: The original shop of one of the better-known chains here, with half a dozen restaurants. Try the mentaiko-shiso monja with cod roe and perilla, which tastes oh so much better than it looks.

candidates.name: Sukiyabashi Jiro
candidates.hours: 11:30-14:00, 17:30-20:30 (Closed Sat evenings, Sundays, public holidays, New Year's holiday and mid-August)
candidates.content: This three Michelin star restaurant and its owner/chef, Jiro Ono, were immortalized in the 2011 documentary Jiro Dreams of Sushi. The highly expensive course is omakase only - Jiro himself selects 20 nigiri pieces daily based on t

candidates.name: Chin Mar Ya
candidates.content: This local fast-food chain started here and serves good, cheap, and spicy maboudofu or Szechuan-style spicy tofu. Though the original restaurant closed in 2022, there are two other locations in Gotanda. Take out also available.

candidates.name: Daigo
candidates.content: Exquisite vegetarian or vegan "shojin ryori" cuisine. This is the traditional Buddhist spin on kaiseki. Gracefully served by attentive kimono-clad staff. Small private dining rooms look out onto Japanese gardens. Very expensive, b

candidates.name: Kongariya
candidates.content: Select from a wide range of onigiri with interesting fillings like squid and kimchee, miso or shoyu grilled riceballs, or even ones wrapped in Indian naan and baked.

candidates.name: Martiniburger
candidates.content: This restaurant serves hamburgers and martinis. The large juicy hamburgers are made with high quality ground beef, which is very hard to find anywhere in Japan. Though uncommon, the combination of hamburgers and martinis is surpri

candidates.name: Okina An
candidates.content: One of the most authentic soba places in Tokyo. The owner keeps the place clean but has not renovated anything since the Showa era. Note the cash register from the 1960s and the museum-worth tea hearth. Try negiseiro, which is buc

candidates.name: Yayoiken
candidates.price: Morning sets from ¥350, full meals from ¥580
candidates.content: Cheap and cheerful grills served on a hot teppan iron plate, with all the rice you can eat. Plastic food models plus a coupon machine with pictures make ordering easy.

candidates.name: Gachapon Hall
candidates.alt: ガチャポン会館 Gachapon kaikan
candidates.content: An entire store full of gachapon: capsule toy vending machines. Put in a few coins, turn the crank, and out pops a capsule containing a random trinket. The small toys and figurines, some of which attach to your keys or phone case,

candidates.name: Setagaya Boro-Ichi
candidates.content: A flea market that's held on the 15th and 16th of December and January each year. It's been drawing shoppers from all over Tokyo since it started in 1578. The main attraction is used clothing (such as kimono) and antiques.

candidates.name: Sugamo
candidates.content: Popularly known as "Grandma's Harajuku" (obaachan no Harajuku), and indeed most shops in the area do seem targeted towards an older clientèle. For the (rare) tourist, however, this means a plentiful supply of tea, pottery, kitchen

candidates.name: Ameyoko
candidates.content: A packed shopping bazaar full of stalls selling almost anything you can imagine. It runs roughly south of Ueno station along the inside of the JR Yamanote line tracks to Okachimachi station. If you are looking for a more typically

candidates.name: Seijo Ishii
candidates.content: The supermarket chain has a store in La Qua, with many imported foods and wines. Many frozen products are sold in restaurant packs.

Snow is rare, but on those rare occasions once every few years when Tokyo is hit by a snowstorm, much of the

Most train lines in Tokyo run 05:00–01:00. During peak hours they run about once every three minutes; even during off-peak hours it's less than ten minutes between trains. The only night when regular passenger services run overnight is for the New Year's Holiday on select lines.

Another option is to choose a cycling tour with a company. This can be a great way to get on a bike and see the best parts of Japan by bicycle. Within Tokyo Soshi's Tokyo Bike Tour, Tokyo Great Cycling Tour, and Bicycle Tours Tokyo offer day tours of popular sites within central Tokyo by bike. For an escape into the ru

Hijiri-bashi Bridge: On the Kanda river (神田川), on the border between Bunkyō and Chiyoda wards. It offers one of the best spots in Tokyo to see trains, three lines crossing each other (on the west, so better seen in the afternoon). Akihabara district in 500 m/10 min away to the east. Its name means Sa

There are no restrictions on entry regardless of religious belief or background.

Yasukuni Shrine: A controversial shrine to Japan's war dead, housing the souls of some 2.5 million people killed in Japan's wars — including convicted war criminals executed by the Allies. A favorite haunt of right-wing groups in black loudspeaker-equipped trucks, and often visited by Japan

Yebisu Brewery Tokyo: A mildly interesting permanent exhibition covering the brewing process in general and the history of Japan Beer Brewery Company which developed Yebisu beer, and which is now a part of Sapporo Breweries. There is even a Virtual Brewery Adventure to try.

During Christmas, Ginza's streets are illuminated. 126 trees in Ginzanamiki street are decorated with 75 thousand light bulbs, and 76 trees in Hanatsubaki street are decorated 35 thousand light bulbs which are made in the shape of stars. The illuminations are turned on on November 15.

Nearby Yoyogi Park (代々木公園 Yoyogi-kōen) was the site of the first successful powered aircraft flight in Japan, on December 19, 1910, by Captain Yoshitoshi Tokugawa, following which it became an army parade ground.
